opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important way to look at it, and it's something people sometimes resist, because there's this appealing idea that a chart is just a neutral window onto the data. You plot the numbers, and the truth sort of appears. But every visualization involves a long chain of choices: what data you collect in the first place, what you leave out, how you aggregate, what you put on the x-axis versus the y-axis, where the baseline is, what colors you use, what you label and what you leave unlabeled. Each of those choices nudges the viewer toward seeing certain things and not others. So in that sense a visualization is always making an argument, even when it doesn't look like it.

I don't think that's a bad thing, though. Rhetoric has a bit of a negative connotation, as if it means manipulation, but the older sense is really just the art of communicating persuasively and clearly. A good visualization designer is thinking about the audience: what do they already know, what question do they bring, what's the one thing I want them to walk away understanding? That's rhetorical thinking, and it's what makes the difference between a chart that just sits there and one that actually changes how someone understands a situation.

Where it gets interesting is that there's a spectrum. On one end you have explanatory graphics, like what you'd see in a newspaper, where the author has a point and the job is to make it vivid and honest. On the other end you have exploratory tools, where you're handing people the data and letting them find their own stories. Fernanda Viégas and I spent a lot of time on that exploratory side, building things where people could upload and play with their own data, and even there the rhetoric doesn't disappear. The design of the tool shapes what kinds of patterns people notice and what kinds of conversations they have. We saw people argue with each other, build on each other's discoveries, essentially use visualizations as moves in a conversation. That social dimension made the rhetorical nature really obvious to us.

So I'd say the responsible stance isn't to pretend you're neutral. It's to be aware of the choices you're making, to make them in good faith, and ideally to give viewers enough context, or enough ability to interact, that they can check your argument rather than just accept it.

r001.rationale: It says choices about what data to collect and what to leave out shape what viewers see, and that a visualization is making an argument.

r002.rationale: It does not mention choosing date boundaries for a time-series chart or how those boundaries affect the message.

r003.rationale: It does not describe truncating a bar chart’s value axis or making small differences appear large.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, "rhetorical" is exactly the right word, and it's one that people in the field sometimes resist, because there's this ideal of visualization as a neutral window onto the data. You just show the numbers, the truth speaks for itself. And I think that's a kind of useful fiction, but it is a fiction.

Every chart involves choices. What goes on the x-axis, what gets aggregated, what gets left out, what color means "bad." Those are arguments. If I show you a line chart of temperature starting in 1880, I'm making a different claim than if I start it in 1998. Neither one is lying, exactly, but each one is telling you what to pay attention to. And the viewer mostly doesn't experience it as an argument. They experience it as seeing. That's what makes visualization so powerful and also a little dangerous: the persuasion happens below the level where people would normally put up their guard.

So the way I've come to think about it is that a good visualization is more like a good essay than like a photograph. There's a point of view. The question isn't whether you have one, it's whether you're honest about it, and whether the view you've constructed actually lets the reader push back. Can they find the thing that contradicts your story if it's there? A chart that makes the counterargument invisible is a bad chart, even if every pixel is technically accurate.

And I'd add that this goes double for the work we've done with machine learning. When you visualize what's going on inside a model, there's often no "ground truth picture" to compare against. You're constructing a lens, and the lens shapes what questions people even think to ask. So I try to be pretty explicit with myself: what am I trying to convince someone of, and what would it look like if I were wrong? If the visualization can't show me being wrong, I don't trust it yet.

r001.rationale: The response says choices about what to include or leave out in a chart are arguments.

r002.rationale: It says a temperature line chart starting in 1880 makes a different claim than one starting in 1998.

r003.rationale: It does not mention bar charts or explain how truncating a value axis can magnify apparent differences.

astra-6.text:
I think visualization is rhetorical almost by definition, because you’re making choices about what people should pay attention to. You choose the data, you choose what to leave out, and you choose how to encode it. Even something as simple as where an axis starts can change the impression someone takes away. So there isn’t really a neutral view from nowhere.

But I’d distinguish making an argument from manipulating somebody. A visualization can make a point and still give you room to question it—to see uncertainty, to look at exceptions, or to explore the data yourself. That’s one of the interesting things about interactive visualization: you can offer a particular perspective, but also give the viewer some ability to push back.

So for me, the question is less, “Is this rhetorical?” and more, “What argument is it making, and does it give the audience a fair chance to assess that argument?”

sol-6.1.text:
I think visualization is rhetorical almost by definition, because you’re making choices about what someone is going to see. You choose the data, you choose what to leave out, you choose the scale and the visual encoding. All of those decisions direct attention and shape the story someone takes away.

That doesn’t mean a visualization has to be misleading. It means that simply saying, “I’m showing the data,” doesn’t get you out of responsibility for those choices. A useful question is: What does this representation make easy to notice, and what does it make hard to notice?

And there’s an interesting tension between explanation and exploration. Sometimes you want to make a particular argument very clearly. Other times you want to give people something they can investigate, where they might discover something you didn’t anticipate. Even then, you’ve designed the space in which they’re exploring. So I think the goal is to be conscious of that framing and give people enough context to question it.
